facts.statement: Anhanguera lived during the Early Cretaceous (112 to 100 million years ago) in Brazil and the Late Cretaceous (98 to 93 million years ago) in Morocco.
facts.quote: Anhanguera () is a genus of pterodactyloid pterosaur known from the Early Cretaceous (Albian age, 112 to 100 million years ago) Romualdo Formation of Brazil (precisely in Araripe Basin) and the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian age, 98 to 93 million years ago) Kem Kem Group of Morocco.

facts.statement: The name Anhanguera is derived from Tupi words meaning "spirit protector of the animals" and "bygone".
facts.quote: The generic name comes from the Tupi words añanga, meaning "spirit protector of the animals" + wera "bygone".

facts.statement: Anhanguera was a fish-eating pterosaur with a wingspan of approximately 4.6 meters.
facts.quote: Anhanguera was a fish-eating animal with a wingspan of about 4.6 m.

facts.statement: Anhanguera possessed rounded crests on the front of its upper and lower jaws filled with angled, conical, and curved teeth.
facts.quote: Like many other anhanguerids, Anhanguera had rounded crests at front of its upper and lower jaws, which were filled with angled, conical but curved teeth of various sizes and orientations.

facts.statement: A 2003 study indicated that Anhanguera held its head at an angle to the ground to aid balance detection via its inner ear structure.
facts.quote: A study in 2003 showed that Anhanguera held its head at an angle to the ground due to its inner ear structure, which helped the animal detect its balance.

facts.statement: Anhanguera had bony scleral rings in its eye sockets that likely provided structural support to the eyes.
facts.quote: Anhanguera had bony rings in their eye sockets, called scleral rings. These disks may have provided support to the pterosaur's eyes.

facts.statement: The type species Anhanguera blittersdorffi is based on a complete skull found in the Romualdo Formation of Brazil.
facts.quote: The type species, A. blittersdorfi, is based on a complete skull from the Romualdo Formation calcareous concretions (Santana Group) of the Ceará and Pernambuco states of Brazil.

facts.statement: The species A. piscator was previously assigned to Coloborhynchus but was later reclassified into Anhanguera by Andres and Myers.
facts.quote: The species A. piscator, known from a nearly-complete skeleton, was at one point proposed to belong to the genus Coloborhynchus, but has more recently been placed back into Anhanguera by Andres and Myers.

facts.statement: In 1986, Rafael Gioia Martins-Neto named a pterosaur "Pricesaurus megalodon" in a lecture at a scientific meeting in São Paulo.
facts.quote: In 1986, Rafael Gioia Martins-Neto reported the find of a pterosaur that he named "Pricesaurus megalodon" in a lecture during the 38th annual meeting of Sociedade Brasileira para o Progresso da Ciência at São Paulo.

facts.statement: Alexander Kellner concluded in 1988 that Pricesaurus was a nomen vanum because the specimens likely represented different individuals.
facts.quote: However, in 1988, Alexander Kellner concluded that Pricesaurus was a nomen vanum, primarily because the specimens almost certainly represented different individuals.

facts.statement: The discovery of Anhanguera helped resolve the debate regarding whether pterosaurs walked on two or four legs.
facts.quote: El descubrimiento de este pterosaurio ayudó a finalizar el debate sobre si los pterosaurios caminaban a dos o cuatro patas.

facts.statement: Anhanguera is closely related to Ornithocheirus and belongs to the family Ornithocheiridae within the subfamily Anhanguerinae.
facts.quote: Estos pterosaurios están cercanamente emparentados con el ornitoqueiro, y pertenecen a su misma familia Ornithocheiridae en una subfamilia propia, Anhanguerinae, que también incluye al Ludodactylus.

facts.statement: Fragments of Anhanguera have been found in Queensland, Australia, while species like A. cuvieri and A. fittoni were found in England.
facts.quote: A. cuvieri y A. fittoni, que inicialmente se habían descrito pertenecientes al género Pterodactylus y posteriormente a Ornithocheirus, son de un periodo un poco posterior al (Albiense) en Inglaterra, mientras que fragmentos de un pterosaurio que puede atribuirse a Anhanguera se han encontrado en Queensland, Australia.

facts.statement: The species A. cuvieri was originally described by Bowerbanks in 1851 and has been synonymized with Ornithocheirus cuvieri and Pterodactylus cuvieri.
facts.quote: A. cuvieri (Bowerbanks 1851) = Ornithocheirus cuvieri = Pterodactylus cuvieri

facts.statement: The species A. fittoni was originally described by Owen in 1858 and is synonymous with Pterodactylus fittoni.
facts.quote: A. fittoni (Owen 1858) = Pterodactylus fittoni Owen 1858

facts.statement: The species A. araripensis was described by Wellnhofer in 1985 and is also classified as Coloborhynchus.
facts.quote: A. araripensis (Wellnhofer 1985) = Santanadactylus araripensis Wellnhofer 1985 [también clasificado como Coloborhynchus]

facts.statement: The species A. blittersdorffi, described by Campos and Kellner in 1985, serves as the type species and is also classified as Coloborhynchus.

facts.statement: The species A. santanae was described by Wellnhofer in 1985 and is synonymous with Araripesaurus santanae.

facts.statement: The species A. robustus was described by Wellnhofer in 1987 and is also classified as Coloborhynchus.
facts.quote: A. robustus (Wellnhofer 1987) = Tropeognathus robustus Wellnhofer 1987 [también clasificado como Coloborhynchus]

facts.statement: The species A. ligabuei was described by Dalla Vecchia in 1993 and is also classified as Coloborhynchus or Cearadactylus.

facts.statement: The species A. piscator was described by Kellner and Tomida in 2000 and is also classified as Coloborhynchus.

facts.statement: The species A. spielbergi was described by Veldmeijer in 2003 and is also classified as Coloborhynchus.

facts.statement: The genus Anhanguera belongs to the parent group Ornithocheiroidea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Ornithocheiroidea

facts.statement: Anhanguera is classified within the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Anhanguera lived from the Valanginian to the Cenomanian stages, between 137.05 and 93.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Valanginian to Cenomanian (137.05 to 93.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: A 2003 study claims that Anhanguera kept their heads tilted relative to the horizontal, based on inner ear structure that helped them maintain balance similarly to humans.
facts.quote: Un estudio de 2003 afirma que los Anhanguera mantenían su cabeza inclinada respecto a la horizontal, según muestra la estructura de su oído interno, que ayudaba al animal a mantener el equilibrio de forma similar a como ocurre en los humanos.
